source.title: Scaling Laws for Precision
source.authors: Tanishq Kumar; Zachary Ankner; B. Spector; Blake Bordelon; Niklas Muennighoff; Mansheej Paul; Cengiz Pehlevan; Christopher Ré; Aditi Raghunathan

record.file_problem: not stated; the supplied text appears to contain the full paper and appendices.
record.tranche_reason: The study measures validation-loss scaling while varying precision and fits or evaluates scaling-law predictions. This is a conceptual test and extension of loss-scaling claims, rather than a reproduction of the original parameter/data/compute experiments.
record.gate_note: The paper reports many post-training-quantization degradation results; rows r11–r13 record the explicit degradation trends, but link them to none of the versions because they measure inference-time quantization degradation rather than the versions’ stated pretraining-loss behavior. The paper also cites scaling results from other work; those cited results are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The study trains 465 OLMo-style LMs and fits a Chinchilla-form loss law in N and D, extended with precision through an effective parameter count. Its results bear on whether that form fits (V1), how training precision shifts the compute-optimal N/D split (V7), and, weakly, on extrapolating to larger compute-matched runs (V2). It is a new setting (low-precision training) rather than a reproduction, so T3, not T2.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct; it should add the authors' further findings. PTQ degradation rises with data, so extra pretraining data can eventually hurt a quantized model. Training precision can be modelled as reducing effective parameter count within a Chinchilla form. Compute-optimal training precision is roughly 7–8 bits and independent of compute, except when N is fixed, where it grows about as log C. The authors call the trends suggestive rather than prescriptive.
record.recipe_differences: This is a precision-scaling study, not a replication of the original parameter/data/compute scaling experiments. It varies training and inference precision, fits effective-parameter and quantization-degradation terms, and derives compute implications from those fits.
record.method_sensitivity: The appendix reports that alternative functional forms produce different fit scores; an alternative C4/hyperparameter setting retains the qualitative precision trend. The study also notes fitted constants can vary with architecture and dataset, but cites other work for that statement.

fits_no_version.finding: Post-training quantization degradation grows with D/N across GPTQ, AWQ and round-to-nearest; larger models degrade less.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Inference-time PTQ loss degradation of BF16-trained LMs rises roughly as a power of the token/parameter ratio.

fits_no_version.finding: When N, D and P are optimized jointly, compute-optimal precision is compute-independent (about 7–8 bits). With N fixed, P* grows roughly as log C.
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Compute-optimal training precision is constant under joint optimization and grows as log compute when model size is fixed.

fits_no_version.finding: Precision effects are well modelled as a saturating-exponential reduction of the effective parameter count, and this form is chosen among alternative precision-term forms on held-out R².
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Low training precision acts as a multiplicative reduction in effective parameters within the Chinchilla form.

record.problems: The main scaling suite uses a fixed architecture and relatively small models (30M–220M parameters) over a limited parameter range. The paper says its compute-optimal allocations are derived from fitted functions and verified numerically, rather than through a broad empirical sweep of allocations across compute budgets. The authors also state that they do not evaluate downstream tasks and that numerical fitted constants depend on setup.
record.rows_left_out: No separate rows for the many individual model-size/data/precision points in Figures 2–7; the paper reports several results as aggregate fits or trends, which are recorded as such. Other precision ablations and plots in Appendices I, L, and N were not separately recorded where they repeat the same qualitative trend without a distinct result tied to a claim version.

untested.parts: Power-law behaviour over several orders of magnitude in N or compute; the sweep covers N 30M–220M and D 1.5–26B.
Prediction of runs orders of magnitude larger; validation reaches only about 8x in N (up to 1.7B).
Any empirical IsoFLOP or allocation sweep. The analytical equal split follows from the imposed α=β tie.
Not tested; a fixed architecture is used throughout.
Not tested; text LM pretraining only (PTQ is inference-time, not fine-tuning or transfer).
Not tested; the authors state there are no downstream evaluations.
Effects of parameter counting, schedule, data or fitting method on the N/D exponents. The study only cites others (Besiroglu, Sardana) for constants varying.

missing.what: Compute-matched floating-point runs from FP4/1.76B to FP32/220M on 16B tokens, compared against integer-fit predictions; the optimum lies near 7–8 bits and loss values are given in Figure 1 right.
missing.locator: Section 4.3.2, Figure 6; Figure 1 right; Appendix J

missing.what: Numerically solved inference-cost model in which N* and D* grow as power laws in inference compute, with P* ∝ log C.

record.verdict_notes: The study is not an original source for any version. The Chinchilla N/D form is largely assumed and extended rather than stress-tested: N spans under one order of magnitude and α=β is tied. The record's V3 labels are removed because the equal allocation exponents are imposed by the tie. The record's V7 label on r6 is moved: those forms concern the precision term only. Peer-review venue in the record (ICLR 2024) is not stated in the text.

versions.untested_parts: The study varies parameter count over 30M–220M and data over 1.5B–26B tokens in its main suite; it does not test the claimed behavior over several orders of magnitude in parameter count, nor compute scaling with precision held otherwise unconstrained.

The paper compares fitted predictions with observed losses, including across integer and floating-point settings, but does not test whether fits from small runs predict runs orders of magnitude larger.

The paper derives compute-optimal parameter/data allocations from its fitted loss form and analyzes precision choices. It does not empirically sweep parameter and token allocations across compute budgets to establish the stated growth trends.
The authors use a fixed architecture and do not compare depth, width, or other architecture choices at fixed parameter count.
The study varies quantization precision in language-model pretraining, but does not test other modalities, repeated data, fine-tuning, or transfer.
The authors explicitly limit their analysis to loss scaling and do not report downstream-task evaluations.

The study compares alternative functional forms and discusses fit choices, but does not independently test how fitted exponents change across architectures or datasets, whether published laws disagree for those reasons, or whether loss curves bend away from a single power law.

rows.subject: OLMo-style models (suite; aggregate scaling-law fit)
rows.operation_detail: Fit validation loss across parameter count, data size, and weight precision using a Chinchilla-form loss with an effective parameter count.

conditions.value: weight precision varied; activations and KV cache held at high precision

rows.measure: Final validation loss; fitted form L(N,D)=A[N(1−e^(−Pw/γw))]^(−α)+BD^(−β)+E
rows.baseline: BF16 or higher-precision reference for the effective-parameter comparison
rows.value: α = 0.4965; α = β in the reported fits. The fitted form is reported in Equation 3.
rows.locator: Sections 2.3 and 4.1; Equations 1 and 3; Appendix K, Table 2
rows.note: The paper describes the effective-parameter form as fitting the observed loss trends; the sweep spans the listed sizes and token budgets.
rows.check: The value is a fitted constant (α=0.4965), and α=β is imposed by tying, not measured. The fit spans only N=30M–220M (under one order of magnitude) and D=1.5–26B. The Figure 4 fit quality is described in words only.

source_check.locator_found: Sections 2.3 and 4.1; Equation 3; Figure 4; Appendix K, Table 2; Appendix M.

rows.subject: OLMo-style models (suite; aggregate precision-combination fit)
rows.operation_detail: Compare joint and marginal fits for combined weight, activation, and KV-cache precision effects.

conditions.value: weights, activations, and KV cache varied individually or in combinations
joint fit versus combined marginal fits

rows.measure: Predicted versus actual final validation loss
rows.value: Joint fit: MSE 0.0086, R² 0.9006; combined marginals: MSE 0.0089, R² 0.8973.
rows.note: The text says the two approaches have approximately the same predictive power and treats the multiplicative effective-parameter formulation as a strong fit.
rows.check: Joint versus marginal fitting of the precision factors tests whether precision effects factorize. It does not test the N/D power law, so it bears on no version.

rows.subject: OLMo-style models (floating-point training runs; aggregate)
rows.size_stated: 140 training runs; parameter sizes and token budgets vary
rows.operation_detail: Fit an effective-parameter loss form to floating-point weight precision and compare predictions with observed losses.
rows.value: MSE 0.0027, R² 0.9678; fitted γw = 2.8111 and exponent bias b = 0.1240.
rows.note: The text describes the functional form as a good fit for these floating-point runs.
rows.check: A, B, E and α are taken from the integer fit; only γw and the bias b are refit. The R² of 0.9678 reflects the floating-point precision term, not N/D scaling.

rows.subject: Fitted loss model (analytical compute-optimal allocation)
rows.operation_detail: Optimize parameter and token allocation at fixed compute with training precision held fixed.
rows.measure: Optimal parameter and data scaling with compute
rows.baseline: Chinchilla-optimal NCh(C) and DCh(C) at full precision
rows.value: N*(P,C) ∝ C^(β/(α+β)); D*(P,C) ∝ C^(α/(α+β)) at fixed P. The paper ties α = β in its reported fits.
rows.note: This is an analytical optimum derived from the fitted loss form, not an empirical sweep of compute budgets.
rows.check: Analytical result. Equation 6 shows that the ratios N*/NCh and D*/DCh depend on training precision P, so the compute-optimal split shifts with a setup choice. For V3 the equal growth exponents follow from the imposed α=β tie, so the row cannot test V3.

rows.subject: Fitted loss model (joint compute-optimal allocation)
rows.operation_detail: Jointly optimize parameter count, token count, and precision under a fixed compute constraint.
rows.measure: Compute dependence of optimal precision and implied parameter/data allocation
rows.value: The optimal precision satisfies a compute-independent implicit equation; the paper reports a fitted optimum around 7–8 bits.
rows.locator: Section 4.3.2, Equation 7 and Finding 3; Appendix E.2.3
rows.note: The analysis supports a fixed precision in this unconstrained optimization, but does not empirically verify parameter and token growth over multiple compute budgets.
rows.check: The result is that compute-optimal precision is independent of compute. It concerns precision, not the N/D growth rates that V3 names. Move to fits_no_version.

rows.subject: OLMo-style models (aggregate fit comparison)
rows.operation_detail: Compare alternative functional forms for fitting precision-related loss effects.

conditions.value: effective parameters, additive/independent power law, effective data, tied or untied effective parameters and data, or multiplicative power law

rows.measure: Held-out R² and number of fitted parameters
rows.value: Effective parameters: R² 0.82, 3 parameters; additive/independent power law: 0.71, 2; effective data: 0.74, 3; tied effective parameters and data: 0.79, 3; untied: 0.84, 4; multiplicative power law in N and P: 0.75, 2.
rows.note: The authors say several forms can be reasonable fits and discuss interpretability and parameter count in choosing among them; the candidates do not all have the same predictive fit.
rows.check: The alternative forms compared are for the precision term, not for the N/D exponents or the compute-optimal split. This is not V7 as stated. The state is better read as a descriptive comparison.

rows.subject: OLMo-style models (alternative hyperparameter/data ablation; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Repeat precision-loss trend measurements with alternative training hyperparameters and a different dataset.

conditions.value: weight decay 1e-3, Adam ε 1e-10, peak learning rate 1e-4, warmup 3%

rows.measure: Final validation loss trend as precision increases
rows.value: The text reports the same qualitative trend: a rapid loss decrease when precision initially increases from 4 bits, followed by diminishing returns at higher precision.
rows.note: The authors say this smaller-scale ablation suggests the precision trends are robust to the tested hyperparameter choices.
rows.check: The hyperparameter/C4 ablation checks the robustness of the precision trend at N=30M, D=1.5B. No scaling-law constants are fit, so it bears on no version.

rows.subject: OLMo-style models (suite; aggregate)
rows.operation_detail: Measure validation-loss degradation after GPTQ post-training weight quantization.
rows.measure: Validation-loss degradation relative to the end of training
rows.baseline: Loss at the end of training before post-training quantization
rows.value: Degradation increases with training data across all model sizes; for fixed dataset size, larger models incur smaller degradation. The degradation fit has R² = 0.97 over all fitted points.
rows.note: This is a post-training quantization result, not a result about pretraining-loss scaling as specified by V1–V7.

rows.value: The authors state that the degradation result is replicated; plotted values are not stated in the text.
rows.note: The appendix says AWQ and round-to-nearest quantization share the reported data-scaling failure mode.

rows.operation_detail: Repeat the post-training quantization degradation analysis using round-to-nearest quantization.
rows.measure: Validation loss after quantization and degradation
rows.value: The authors state that the degradation result is replicated; plotted values are not stated in the text.
rows.note: The appendix reports the same qualitative data-scaling failure mode as for GPTQ.

rows.operation_detail: Optimize precision and data at fixed parameter count under fixed compute.

relationships.condition: Integer-type OLMo-style models, 30M–220M parameters, 1.5–26B tokens, varied weight precision
relationships.reason: A single Chinchilla-form fit with N replaced by Neff tracks final validation loss across N, D and Pw (Figure 4) (r1). The range is narrow and α=β is tied by choice.
relationships.display_finding: A Chinchilla-form fit using effective parameters tracked final validation loss across model size, tokens and weight precision, with parameter and data exponents constrained equal.

source_check.condition: Integer-type OLMo-style models, 30M–220M parameters, 1.5–26B tokens, varied weight precision
source_check.reason: Equation 3 and Figure 4 support the effective-parameter power-law form within this tested range. Several-order scaling is untested; equality of the exponents is imposed.

relationships.condition: Compute-optimal allocation under C ∝ NDP with training precision as a setup variable
relationships.reason: Equation 6 makes N*/NCh and D*/DCh depend on precision: lower precision favours more parameters and less data (r4). The compute-matched floating-point runs in Figure 6, not yet a row, show the loss optimum shifting from BF16/440M toward lower precision and larger N; this is drawn from the text.
relationships.display_finding: Lower precision favors more parameters and fewer training tokens, with matched-compute runs shifting the loss optimum from BF16/440M toward lower precision and larger models.

relation.reason: Its experiments test an effective-parameter extension of the loss law and predictions across model sizes and precision representations.

tranche.reason: Tests loss scaling in a new precision setting through quantized pretraining, post-training quantization, and precision-dependent compute allocation.

source_check.notes: The transfer experiment changes precision representation and reaches only 8× the largest fitting model, so orders-of-magnitude extrapolation remains untested. Section 4.3.2 says 1.6B, whereas Figures 1 and 6 label the largest model 1.76B.

statements.correction: Section 4.3.2: FP4–FP32 transfer experiment; integer-fit predictions agree strongly until 4-bit precision, where type differences become more apparent. Figure 6: predictions shifted upward relative to floating-point observations; largest plotted model 1.76B.
statements.problem: The larger-scale transfer experiment reaches FP4, not below 4 bits. The paper describes a more apparent discrepancy at 4 bits, while qualitative trends continue to match.

statements.correction: Section 4.3.2 and Figure 6: upward prediction offset; discrepancy more apparent at 4-bit precision; tested floating-point range FP4–FP32.
statements.problem: Imperfect transfer between integer and floating-point representations is supported, but the stated below-4-bit boundary is unsupported by this experiment.
